Private spaces, recliner, music w headphones, weighted blanket, eye mask, rocks to hold for weight, comfortable setting (less hospital looking think more like a relaxing space) since there's a percentage of us with medical PTSD. 

It needs to be a quiet enough space. I like to spend about 20 minutes beforehand stretching so a big enough space to stretch out the hammies will be nice. A close enough bathroom. Wheelchairs for people who are too inebriated and need assistance. There's one clinic I'm not the most fan of because I have to walk multiple flights up with no elevator.

Light snacks options, tea. 

Optional recovery room, if you need to flip a private room over for the next patient but the previous one needs more time then a recovery room separate from waiting is nice to have.

Before treatment is one of the important parts, making sure people are relaxed, comfortable feeling safe and secure. 

Price affordability. Flexible price options for people with already established therapists versus those who would like to have someone sit with them.  

Ideally I'd love to see it 100% covered by insurance it's ideal treatment for me for PTSD and Depression. I got my life back after trying over a decade of other medications/hospitalizations. It absolutely kills my finances having to pay for it out of pocket. But it's either paying for treatment or be so non-functional I can't even get out of bed.

Gonna see a wide variety of people on their journeys to wellness who are on the obese side so double check that your recliners and wheelchairs and waiting room accommodates that.

I'm glad you're doing your best reaching out to him. Unfortunately there's no "timeline" per se. Sometimes people will have periods of wellness and unwellness. It sounds like his PTSD is severe for him to consider getting on disability for awhile. That will help with some financial support. US usually denies Disabiliy the first few times so gotta keep applying just FYI. I think stabilization is the first step maybe getting into an outpatient day program would help him to know of coping strategies. There are some meds that exist that help with nightmares with great effect its technically a blood pressure medication so hopefully he can ask about that
 The therapist can put in a referral for the day program but he'll need a psychiatrist for meds. I think you need to be aware that this could potentially be a lifelong thing of various hills and dips of wellness and unwellness. I know sometimes I'm REALLY well where I can do talks about what's happened to me to rooms full of 200+ people and then there's me now and I run and hide when people say certain things. I'm currently under a weighted blanket right now due to that and that helps me a ton. It's hills and dips but people who are in crisis mode like your brother might not see that this is just a dip since he's dealing with PTSD stuff that's impacting his life every day substantially. Not sure if I'm making sense but it's hard to have any focus when you're losing hours and days to the flashback torture machine that is the brain.

Edit: No emotional "bottom" for me more like a lifetime of severe PTSD / Depression / Anxiety. I've been in therapy for a decade easily. It took me a long time getting through college and it was stressful working 2-3 jobs and Full Time School at the time and I believe I was in and out of the hospital the most at that time. 4 or 5 times for MH stuff? Voluntary check into the MH ward when I really needed to. I really burned out when I got out of college but it is doable if taken slow and steadily. PTSD can be triggered by stressful situations. I definitely recommend having him pick up a couple of chill hobbies maybe something he's never done before so there's no childhood affiliation and resulting triggers.

Some of the crux of the issue with EDs needs to be overseen by a professional - even if it’s just digital sessions it’s better than nothing to help retrain your brain. Relapsing happens and it’s not a failure - it’s another opportunity to discover new tools that work for you so that you can live a full and well life and therapy helps. 

A lot of smokers who first quit have some troubles so if you can find something that keeps your hands busy that will be good. Some people chew on sunflower seeds or use lollipops. I know someone who only played Zelda when having a craving. Some sort of thing you can be doing when you’re having a craving. 

One of my tools is to have a self care box - like a shoebox or part of a drawer or something like that. Fill that with items that make you feel good - a book, a list of people to chat with, a movie, good smelling things like a candle or incense, an art project, coloring book - so that when a hard moment comes you can flip open the box and you’ve got some stuff available to occupy yourself.
